subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: retaliating by leaking something back [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. A private photo of Sumit was passed around the year group. He was sure it was a classmate who'd been rude to him all term.
Tuesday. Rage sat in his chest like a stone. That evening he found an embarrassing picture of that classmate and posted it in a big group chat, with a mocking line. It got forty reactions in an hour. For a few minutes it felt like winning.
Thursday. Minakshi ma'am, the year head, called Sumit in. The classmate's parents had complained. “Your photo being shared was wrong, and we are dealing with it,” she said. “But what you posted is wrong too, and it may count against you.” Sumit stared at his shoes. He had turned from the one wronged into the one explaining himself.

qa.q: Who did Sumit think had shared his photo?
qa.a: A classmate who had been rude to him all term.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling on Tuesday evening when he posted the picture?
qa.a: Rage and hurt, and a need to hit back, which briefly felt like winning.

qa.q: What could Sumit have done instead of posting, and why?
qa.a: Save proof and tell a teacher or parent, since that keeps him as the person who was wronged and lets adults act.

qa.q: How does the situation look to the classmate?
qa.a: The classmate now has something to point at and can claim to be the one wronged, and is also embarrassed and upset by the posted picture.

grounding: A student retaliates by posting an embarrassing picture of the classmate he suspects, turning himself from victim into wrongdoer.

subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: retaliating by leaking something back [Pitfall]
passage:
Leela, you're angry, and I understand. But before you post anything back, let me tell you what I did at your age.
In Class Ten, someone put a photo of me on a social page, sweaty and red-faced after I fell in the relay, with a nasty caption. I was sure it was Deepesh, the boy who sat behind me. So that same night I found a photo of him asleep on the school bus, mouth open, and posted it with something worse.
By morning, everything flipped. The school didn't ask about my photo first; they asked about his. Deepesh's parents complained. My father sat in the principal's office and said, “Jagdish, what have you done?” The principal said my post could itself count as an offence. And whoever posted mine said, “He did worse,” and got off lightly.
I never even found out if it was Deepesh. So, Leela, give me your phone, and let's report it properly, tonight.

qa.q: Where had the photo of Deepesh been taken?
qa.a: Asleep on the school bus, mouth open.

qa.q: What was young Jagdish feeling when he posted the photo of Deepesh?
qa.a: He was angry and humiliated, sure Deepesh was to blame and wanting to hurt him back.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept Jagdish the one who was wronged?
qa.a: Reporting his own photo to the school instead of posting back, which would have kept the focus on whoever started it.

qa.q: How was Deepesh affected by what young Jagdish did?
qa.a: Deepesh was mocked in public, perhaps without having done anything, and his parents had to complain to the school.

grounding: An elder recalls posting an embarrassing photo of a suspected classmate, turning from victim into wrongdoer and giving the real poster a defence.

subtopic: Handling a leaked photo or online harassment
subtype: Approach: retaliating by leaking something back [Pitfall]
passage:
It was past midnight, the power gone and the inverter beeping, when Imran made the decision. For three days a meme with his face had been going round the class group, and tonight someone told him Naveen had made it. Imran was sure. By the light of his phone he scrolled through the class trip folder, found a photo of Naveen with his trousers torn at the knee, and posted it with a caption meant to hurt.
By morning the group had turned. Half were laughing at Naveen now. Naveen's parents emailed the school. At the meeting, the vice-principal said Imran's post was a serious matter in itself and might even break the law. Naveen swore he hadn't made the meme, and nobody could prove he had. The student who really made it, it came out later, used Imran's post to say, “He's no better.”
Imran's mother, beside him, held his hand while the vice-principal set out what would happen next.

qa.q: What did Imran post about Naveen?
qa.a: A photo of Naveen with his trousers torn at the knee, with a caption meant to hurt.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he made the decision past midnight?
qa.a: He was furious and humiliated after three days of the meme, and sure enough of Naveen's guilt to strike back.

qa.q: What could Imran have done that night instead?
qa.a: Screenshot the meme and show his mother and the school in the morning, so whoever made it would be the one answering for it.

qa.q: How was the morning for Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen was mocked in front of the class and had to deny something nobody could prove, which must have felt deeply unfair.

grounding: Shows a student posting an embarrassing photo of the classmate he suspects, becoming a wrongdoer himself and giving the real harasser a defence.
